item.title: Avenda Health expands Unfold AI platform to support intraoperative prostate cancer care
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Surgery Mode in Unfold AI brings patient-specific 3D maps to give an enhanced view of cancer anatomy during robotic prostate procedures.

The post Avenda Health expands Unfold AI platform to support intraoperative prostate cancer care appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Unfold AI is designed to help physicians identify cancerous tissue. Source: Avenda Health

Prostate treatment has improved with robotics, and it could improve again soon with artificial intelligence. Avenda Health today announced Surgery Mode, a new suit of interoperative features for its Unfold AI offering. The multimodal AI-powered prostate cancer mapping platform is designed to reveal the true size and extent of disease to help physicians make better informed treatment decisions.

“Our goal with Unfold AI has always been to provide more clinical clarity throughout every stage of a patient’s cancer journey,” stated Shyam Natarajan, Ph.D., co-founder and CEO of Avenda Health.

“Whether a physician is counseling a newly diagnosed patient, planning a targeted radiation oncology treatment, or performing a complex radical prostatectomy, having an accurate 3D map of the disease is transformative,” he added. “These new surgical enhancements empower physicians with the visual confidence needed to achieve optimal cancer control while protecting patient quality of life during complex procedures.”

Founded in 2017, Avenda Health said it is creating a more personalized future of prostate cancer care. With deep learning, the Culver City, Calif.-based company‘s software maps a patient’s cancer in 3D, giving physicians precise information and the confidence to make care decisions. Avenda said it aims to improve outcomes, preserve quality of life, and create a new standard of prostate cancer care.

Avenda Health bases Surgery Mode on research

Avenda Health said it designed Surgery Mode to enhance how surgeons use 3D AI mapping during non-robotic and robotic surgeries, alongside new tools to simplify patient case management and physician workflows.

The launch builds on peer-reviewed research predicting that Unfold AI could cut positive surgical margins in half, substantially reducing cancer recurrence. In the study, the system outperformed MRI and other modalities in assessing whether cancer had spread beyond the prostate, assisting surgeons in making nerve-sparing decisions.

In Surgery Mode, physicians can now access enlarged 3D views for clearer visualization, adjust the cancer estimation map to match the camera angle on the surgical console, review underlying MRI slices during the procedure, and access capsule risk scores from within a dedicated surgical view.

Avenda Health claimed that Unfold AI is the only platform implementing multimodal AI to analyze a patient’s MRI, biopsy, pathology, and PSA together. It produces a personalized 3D map of the cancer’s extent to provide surgeons with more precise visualization of tumor boundaries.

While Unfold AI has served as a decision-support tool during preoperative consultations, the latest expansion gives surgeons an enhanced version of these maps during prostate procedures. The suite of improved workflow tools also gives physicians and staff greater visibility into the status of each patient case.

Key features

  • Aligned Capsule Risk Score mapping: The Capsule Risk Score overlay now automatically flips its left/right visual orientation to mirror the surgical camera view, giving surgeons immediate, color-coded risk feedback by quadrant to guide precise nerve-sparing decisions in real time.
  • Redesigned patient list and case filters: Improved patient organization and updated case status labels let users search for cases in progress, add new patients, and filter by status to see where each case stands at a glance.
  • Improved administrative control: New built-in tools let staff verify insurance approvals and confirm administrative steps are complete before 3D map generation.
  • Streamlined case management: Care teams can now add and view patient notes directly from the patient list and update the assigned physician on a patient report.

Unfold AI helps doctors identify tumor extent

Avenda Health said the expanded features extend Unfold AI’s reach across the prostate cancer care pathway, including active surveillance, focal therapy, surgical interventions, and radiotherapy. Its interactive 3D maps serve as a visual guide for patient counseling and decision support, helping patients and physicians confidently select their treatment path.

Now, with Surgery Mode, the same patient-specific mapping technology can be used to provide clear visual boundaries in the operating room, actively guiding surgical procedures such as robotic prostatectomies.

Unfold AI predicts the cancer’s spread into nearby anatomy with 92% accuracy, compared with 52% using MRI alone. That spatial clarity is central to helping surgeons determine whether a nerve-sparing or non-nerve-sparing surgery should be performed.

Avenda noted that additional research demonstrated that Unfold AI improves physician identification of tumor extent, increasing sensitivity from 37% to 97%. By expanding Unfold AI from preoperative decision support into the operating room, the company said it is developing more precise views of prostate cancer that can support physicians across different stages of care.

item.title: A guide to Day 1 of RoboBusiness 2026
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
We've compiled a schedule for everything happening on the first day of RoboBusiness 2026 in Santa Clara, Calif.

The post A guide to Day 1 of RoboBusiness 2026 appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Today marks the start of RoboBusiness 2026! This year, we’ll be celebrating the 20th anniversary of RoboBusiness with the community that made it possible and looking ahead to more years of collaboration and growth.

The event will start at the Santa Clara Convention Center at 9:15 a.m. PT with the opening keynote, “The Next 20 Years of Robotics.” As RoboBusiness marks its 20th anniversary, industry leaders will reflect on the breakthroughs that defined the past two decades and explore the technologies, markets, opportunities, and challenges that will shape the next 20 years. This year, all keynotes will take place in the theatre on the second floor.

This talk will include Rodney Brooks, the co-founder and CTO of Robust AI; Jonathan Hurst, the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics; and Ken Goldberg, the William S. Floyd Jr Distinguished Chair in Engineering at UC Berkeley.

At 10:00 a.m., the RoboBusiness show floor will open. There, attendees can find interesting robotics demonstrations, the Engineering Theater, and the Startup Alley.

The day will close with another keynote talk, “Beyond the Demo: AI in Production Robotics” at 4:30 p.m. It will include insights from Bhavana Chandrashekhar, the senior manager of applied science at Amazon Robotics; James Davidson, the chief AI officer at Teradyne Robotics; Ali Raja, vice president of data centers at ABB Robotics; Ram Devarajulu, vice president of deep tech innovations at Cambridge Consultants; and Jon Battles, the vice president of technology strategy at Cobot.

After the final keynote, head back to the exhibitor hall for the Networking Reception presented by Harmonic Drive. The reception will include drinks, light appetizers, and time to connect with other RoboBusiness 2026 attendees and speakers.

Registration for the show is available on site.

Morning breakout session schedule

RoboBusiness 2026 breakout sessions will start at 10:30 a.m. upstairs from the show floor. They include:

  • Designing Data Programs for Humans, Not Robots: Aaron Bromberg, the head of robotics and physical AI at Instawork, will explain what it takes to capture usable data from real workers on real shifts, and what he has learned putting camera systems into commercial environments at scale. This talk will be in Room 209/210.
  • Startup Bootcamp Part 1: The Basics to Best Practices: Colleen Anderson, the director of community and events at MassRobotics; John Lanza and Jennifer Audeh, partners at Foley Hoag; and Brooke Fritz, a partner of tech transactions at Foley Hoag, will provide best practices for robotics startups. The session will be in Room 207.
  • Designing the Robotics Ecosystem for Outdoor Autonomy: In this session, Mel Torrie, the CEO of Autonomous Solutions Inc., will explain why the intersection of autonomous vehicles and advanced robotics will further revolutionize field deployments. It will take place in Room 206.
  • The Humanoid Bill of Materials: De-Risking the Multi-Billion Dollar Bottleneck: Michelle Sun, the founder of Core Matter Labs, will strip away the marketing hype to expose the stark economic and geopolitical realities of the physical AI supply chain. The session will be in Room 203.
  • Integrated Drive Actuator Design: Combining Gearheads, Motor, Drive and Sensors for Smarter Motion: Marcel Almonte, a mechatronics applications engineer at Harmonic Drive, will teach attendees how integrated actuators can reduce engineering effort by simplifying system integration, minimizing cabling complexity, shortening testing and commissioning, and accelerating time to market. His session will start at 10:30 a.m.

Sessions starting at 11:30 a.m. include:

  • Why Food is Physical AI’s Hardest Problem & Most Promising Catalyst: Rajat Bhageria, the founder and CEO of Chef Robotics, will explore what makes food such a demanding benchmark for physical AI. This session will be in Room 209/210.
  • Startup Boot Camp Part 2: Challenges & Best Practices for Working with Corporate Partners: Joyce Sidopoulos, co-founder and chief of operations at MassRobotics; Ben Waters, co-founder and CEO of WiBotic; and Colm Prendergast, senior director and head of the Emerging Tech Hub at Analog Devices, will provide actionable strategies for successfully collaborating with corporate partners. The session will take place in Room 207.
  • Deployment Over Demos: Building Risk-Aware Foundation Models for Safety-Critical Environments: In this fireside chat, Andrey Konchenko, the head of product at FieldAI, will describe how a physics-first foundation model designed specifically for physical AI can address long-standing autonomy challenges in robotics. This talk will be in Room 206.
  • A Joint-by-Joint Guide to Humanoid Motion: Yoshi Umeno, the global director of business development for robotics at Kollmorgen, and Reginald Duffus, the supervisor of application engineering at Kollmorgen, will provide a practical framework for evaluating motion partners, highlighting comprehensive solutions and co-engineering support to simplify the path from prototype to volume production. It will be in Room 203.
  • Tactile Sensing Solutions for the Physical AI Era: This panel will include insights from Eric Utley, an applications engineering manager at Protolabs; Ron Zukerman, the director of business development and innovation at VPG; Andrew Gosline, a senior mechatronic systems engineer at Simplexity Product Development; and Dorota Shortell, the CEO of Simplexity Product Development. These experts will discuss how tactile sensing is evolving. It will take place in Room 204.

Plan your afternoon at RoboBusiness 2026

At 12:15 p.m., Bhavana Chandrashekhar, the senior manager of applied science at Amazon Robotics, and Joyce Sidopoulos, co-founder and chief of operations at MassRobotics, will start the Women in Robotics Luncheon. This ticketed event will include a fireside chat between the two tech leaders. It presents an opportunity for women in the industry to form connections, deepen relationships, and champion increased female representation in robotics leadership.

RoboBusiness 2026 beakout sessions will resume in the afternoon. Sessions starting at 1:15 p.m. include:

  • From Models to Machines: Building the Open Infrastructure for Physical AI: Nagesh Puppala, the general manager of physical AI and robotics at Intel, will explore the infrastructure required to move physical AI from prototype to production in real-world robotics systems. The talk will be in Room 209/210.
  • State of Robotics Investments: Sanjay Aggarwal, a venture partner at F-Prime Capital, and Betsy Mulé, a principal at F-Prime, will unveil the firm’s annual “State of Robotics Investments” report, highlighting the latest funding trends, emerging technology categories, and the sectors attracting the most investor interest. The session will take place in Room 207.
  • Closing the Capability Gap: A Leadership Framework for Scaling Field Robotics: Kenrick Tjandra, the robot deployment lead of Raise Robotics, will provide attendees with a decision rule for allocating engineering capacity, a vocabulary for two hidden failure modes, and the pre-mobilization gates that keep field programs from stalling. He will explain the discipline that separates a demo from a system that scales. His talk will be in Room 206.
  • Beyond the Pilot: What It Takes to Put Humanoids to Work in Manufacturing: Dr. Weiwei Chen, the founder and CEO of EmbodyX, will share what the company has learned deploying humanoids in real manufacturing environments. This RoboBusiness 2026 session will be in Room 203.
  • How Robotics and Physical AI are Transforming Modular Data Center Construction: Ali Raja, the vice president of data centers at ABB Robotics, will explore how robotics, prefabrication and modular construction can work together to streamline delivery, reduce pressure on scarce labor and scale data center capacity. The talk will be in Room 204.

Talks starting at 2:15 p.m. include:

  • Physical AI Doesn’t Have a Data Problem; It Has a Deployment Problem: Rudy Cohen, the co-founder and CEO of Inbolt, will reframe where physical AI actually pays off. Cohen said this happens not in bigger models, but in closing the loop at servo frequency and collapsing the months of fixtures, wiring, and retuning that make every deployment a six-figure project. This will take place in Room 209/210.
  • The Economics of Robotics: Is This Business Viable? Jack Pearson, an investment principal at RoboStrategy, will offer a set of mental models for judging whether a robotics business can create real value and capture it in a way that lasts. The session will be in Room 207.
  • Lessons Learned Building Reliable Outdoor Robots: This panel will feature insights from Ben Waters, co-founder and CEO of WiBotic; Vibhor Sood, co-founder and VP of engineering at Burro; Derek Chase, the vice president of robotics and AI at Nextpower; and Ben Choster, the founder of Catalyze Robotics. The panel will demonstrate how engineering decisions impact reliability, uptime, operational efficiency, and total cost of ownership. It will take place in Room 206.
  • A Crash Course in Force & Torque Sensing for Humanoids: Robert Brooks, the founder and CEO of ForceN, will summarize learnings from working with many of world’s top humanoid companies over the past three years. His talk will be in Room 203.
  • Functional Safety for Humanoid Actuators: Jordan Schaeffer, the manager of business development at Novanta, will explore how safe motion, torque control, fault detection, and actuator-level safety functions can help reduce risk while maintaining performance. The talk will take place in Room 204.

RoboBusiness 2026 talks starting at 3:30 p.m. include:

  • How Agentic Coding Empowers Lean Teams to Build Faster: Anthony Jules, the co-founder and chief innovation officer at Robust AI, will explore how AI agents are transforming the robotics development lifecycle right from the initial design phase. The talk will be in Room 209/210.
  • The RaaS Playbook: Pricing, Service & Scale: This panel will include insights from Rick Faulk, the CEO of Locus Robotics; Bill Booth, who leads technology sales, marketing, and business development at Roboworx; and Alex Linde, the chief product officer at Aescape. The speakers will provide attendees with practical strategies for building sustainable RaaS offerings that deliver value for both robotics providers and their customers. The panel will take place in Room 207.
  • Designing Dexterous Learning Robots for Outdoor Labor: Brent Shedd, the founder and CEO of AgRobotics, will deliver a practitioner-level framework: What’s working, what’s hard, and what a realistic path to commercial deployment actually looks like. The talk will be in Room 206.
  • Can Humanoids be Safe? Benjamin Twombly, the founder and CEO of Critical Systems Analysis, will share insights into both the continuity and the evolution of safety thinking as it adapts to intelligent, human-like machines operating in dynamic, real-world contexts. His session will take place in Room 203.
  • What AI-Defined Automation Looks Like in Production: François Giguére, the chief technology officer at Vention, will give attendees a framework for evaluating AI-defined automation in their own operations. The talk will be in Room 204.

Engineering Theater talks

On the show floor, we’ll be running talks in the Engineering Theater throughout the day. The talks include:

  • Sensor Solutions for Humanoids: Tools to Build the Future: Uma Krishnamoorthy, the senior director of core technology at InvenSense, will explore sensing solutions enabling today’s humanoid innovations. Her talk will start at 11:00 a.m.
  • The Robot Out of the Cage. Advanced Functional Safety for Humanoids: Jan Kaiser, the head of marketing at Synapticon, will discuss how certifiable safety architecture will lay a path towards real-world deployments for humanoids. The talk will start at 11:45 a.m.
  • From First Flash to Field Repair: Servicing Robots From a Tablet: Reed Giovannetti, co-founder and CEO of DeviceNexus, will work through the engineering questions behind keeping robots running, on the bench and in the field. This session will begin at 12:30 p.m.
  • Simulation Said Go. The Binary Said No: Keeping Robots Inside Their Requirements in the AI Era: Stojan Gancev, the VP of R&D at Aurora Labs, will discuss the importance of reasoning straight from the architecture, from the compiled binary sitting on the target processor, rather than trusting review and simulation to catch what they structurally cannot see. It will start at 2:00 p.m.
  • Shared Spaces: Navigating Challenges for Indoor Robots: This RoboBusiness 2026 panel session will include insights from Aaron Edsinger, co-founder and CEO of Hello Robot, and Matt Anderson, co-founder and CEO of A&K Robotics. The two will discuss how solving navigation challenges will be critical to achieving broad consumer acceptance and large-scale deployment. It will start at 3:30 p.m.
Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

item.title: Gecko Robotics secures $300M contract with the U.S. Navy
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Gecko claimed this signals the Pentagon’s confidence that it is a core military capability that is delivering results.

The post Gecko Robotics secures $300M contract with the U.S. Navy appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Gecko’s suite of technologies ensures data integrity by collecting and integrating full-coverage, high-fidelity data layers. | Source: Gecko Robotics

Gecko Robotics this week said it has earned an additional $300 million its contract with the U.S. Navy and General Services Administration. With the increase, the U.S. Navy and GSA have quadrupled the ceiling value on Gecko’s contract for slashing maintenance delays and improving fleet readiness. The news came just six months after an initial $71 million IDIQ contract award.

This fourfold expansion will accommodate rapid robotic deployment across the Navy and is one of the strongest public endorsements yet of operational AI and robotics in defense, claimed Gecko Robotics. The Pittsburgh-based company claimed that this showed the Pentagon’s confidence that it is delivering a core military capability of producing results, not experimental technology.

“The conversation around AI and robotics in defense is no longer about experimental technology. It’s about delivering measurable and impactful returns,” said Jake Loosararian, co-founder and CEO of Gecko Robotics.

“With savings of millions of dollars per ship, months of inspections turning into days, and warships returning to sea faster, the U.S. Navy is demonstrating to the world how to deploy technology at scale,” he added. “We’re proud to give our service members the tools they need to stay ahead of emerging threats.”

Gecko said its AI and robotic technology can save the U.S. Navy up to $8 million in repair costs per ship and return vessels to sea quicker. It does this by identifying structural issues up to 50 times faster than traditional methods, reducing inspections from months to days.

Komodo scans through deck coating without stripping them

Central to the expansion is Komodo, a proprietary Gecko robotic technology system. Komodo scans through thick, non-skid deck coatings without stripping or damaging them, giving the Navy the ability to see the health of assets without taking it apart.

It produces a full-deck heatmap of corrosion and material thickness, enabling repair teams to pinpoint damage and plan work before a ship enters drydock, which was previously possible only after maintenance had begun.

The ceiling increase comes as the Department of the Navy places greater emphasis on fleet readiness as a national security priority. Each additional day a warship spends in maintenance reduces its ability to deter adversaries, respond to crises, and project power around the world, said the Navy. The chief of naval operations has set a target of 80% fleet readiness, which Gecko will have a crucial role in helping to meet.

Gecko’s wall-climbing robots, drones, and fixed-sensors collect an unprecedented amount of data on the health of U.S. Navy ships and submarines, including components, hulls, decks and welds, with AI being used to create accurate models to identify any current and future structural issues, even ones that cannot be seen by the human eye.

item.title: Daimon Robotics building the infrastructure layer for tactile intelligence
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
The company is connecting tactile sensing, real-world data collection, simulation, and AI models to help robots perform physical tasks more reliably.

The post Daimon Robotics building the infrastructure layer for tactile intelligence  appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Credit: Daimon Robotics

Vision has become central to modern robotics, but cameras alone cannot tell a robot everything it needs to know about physical contact. When handling flexible objects, inserting components, or manipulating delicate items, robots need information about forces, slippage, and contact that visual systems may miss. 

Daimon Robotics wants to provide the infrastructure to help robots develop that capability. 

Rather than focusing exclusively on tactile sensors or developing a single foundation model, the company is building a pipeline that connects tactile sensing, data collection, simulation, and AI models. Its goal is to turn physical interactions into useful training data that helps robots perform manipulation tasks more reliably. 

“By building tactile intelligence, we’re actually playing the role as an infrastructure provider,” Daimon’s Partner & VP of Technology Dr. Zhu told The Robot Report. “We’re not aiming to be a foundation model developer. We are providing the infrastructure for doing so for those downstream customers.” 

That distinction is central to Daimon’s strategy: develop the tools and data infrastructure that other companies can use to build more capable robotic systems.

Building a pipeline for tactile data

Collecting useful tactile data at scale presents a challenge. Unlike visual data, which can be captured relatively easily with cameras, tactile data depends on physical contact. The resulting information varies with an object’s material, geometry, the forces applied, and the task being performed.

Daimon is developing a pipeline to capture and process these interactions, with tactile feedback operating at 30 Hz. The company is also working to connect real-world data with simulation, allowing physical interactions to inform training in virtual environments. 

The sim-to-real gap remains a significant challenge, particularly when accurately reproducing physical properties such as friction and contact forces. Daimon’s approach starts by calibrating simulations against real-world measurements before transferring collected data into simulated environments. 

“Let’s be frank; it’s not good enough. It’s kind of terrible,” Zhu said of the current state of simulation, referring to the gap between simulated and real-world environments. 

Daimon is developing tactile simulations that account for physical properties measured through real-world testing. The goal is to improve the fidelity of those simulations and make it easier to transfer learned capabilities to physical robots. 

The company has discussed collecting more than 10,000 hours of data, with its longer-term Daimon-Infinity initiative targeting more than 1 million hours of tactile embodied data. 

Zhu also emphasized the importance of working with companies developing robotic models and applications. 

“Doing everything ourselves was not enough,” he said. “Collaborating internationally in different downstream scenarios is really important.”

That collaboration helps Daimon understand what other developers need from its sensors, data-collection devices, software, and evaluation tools.

Credit: Daimon Robotics

From tactile demonstrations to industrial applications

Daimon is targeting manipulation tasks such as assembly and packaging, where robots must respond to physical contact rather than simply follow predetermined trajectories. 

A robot might need to determine whether a component is properly seated, detect when an object slips, or adjust its movements when a part behaves unexpectedly. Tactile feedback can help it respond to these conditions. 

The company demonstrated applications involving delicate manipulation at IROS 2026, including applying heat-transfer designs to tote bags and threading bracelets. It also showed a robot collecting and packaging broken glass, illustrating how models trained on data from varied scenarios can be prompted to perform specific tasks. 

Daimon uses its Umi device to collect data from human interactions. Zhu said the company’s demonstrations were powered by foundation models trained on data collected across multiple scenarios, rather than being built solely around individual robot demonstrations.

The company has identified Lenovo Capital and Inovance Technology as key partners. Zhu said Daimon has also moved beyond proof-of-concept projects into industrial assembly lines and warehouses, although he declined to name specific customers because of nondisclosure agreements. 

The commercial test is whether tactile sensing and the models built around it can improve performance consistently in production environments, where robots must handle variations in objects, materials, and operating conditions. 

Moving beyond visual perception

Daimon’s broader strategy centers on developing models that can use tactile information to understand and respond to physical interactions. 

Its Daimon-TWM effort focuses on a tactile-grounded world model intended to help robots reason about physical interactions, rather than relying on visual perception alone. 

Recognizing an object is only part of manipulation. A robot must also understand how its actions affect that object and adjust when the physical result differs from expectations. Tactile feedback can help close that loop by providing information about contact and the consequences of an action. 

Zhu described two roles for tactile sensing in robotic systems: helping models reason about physical properties and enabling rapid adjustments during contact-intensive tasks. The latter can require high-frequency feedback, with Daimon targeting control at 30 Hz. 

The company is also exploring how data collected through human interactions can help train models for different robot configurations, including humanoids and dual-arm manipulators. 

But collecting data and training models are only part of the problem. Developers must still demonstrate that these systems generalize across different objects, materials, robots, and operating conditions. 

Scaling touch for robotics

The broader question facing the robotics industry is what infrastructure is needed to make physical AI work reliably outside controlled demonstrations. 

Companies are investing heavily in vision-language-action models, simulation, and large-scale robot training datasets. Touch adds another dimension, particularly for robots that must manipulate objects through physical contact. 

Daimon aims to build part of the infrastructure connecting sensing, data, simulation, and intelligence. Its strategy is to support the companies developing robotic systems rather than compete directly with them to build the next general-purpose robotic brain. 

Its success will depend on whether that approach measurably improves manipulation, reduces the effort required to develop new applications, and supports deployments across different industrial environments. 

Zhu was careful not to overstate the capabilities of today’s models. Even when trained on large datasets, he said, their ability to generalize remains limited. 

“The model is not as intelligent as we think,” Zhu said. “It has some generalization ability, but it was in-domain generalization sometimes.”
He added that embodied-intelligence models are still in development, and that collecting data from similar tasks can help them generalize to new applications. 

For Daimon, the challenge is turning that emerging capability into reliable performance across a broader range of real-world tasks.

item.title: Kodama raises $7M to bring robotics to forestry
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Kodama is working on automating forestry and logging equipment, starting with teleoperation and collecting valuable data on the way.

The post Kodama raises $7M to bring robotics to forestry appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Kodama initially focused on wildfire risk reduction in the western U.S., but it is now focusing on the timber industry in the southeastern U.S. | Source: Kodama

Kodama Systems today said it has raised $7 million to bring physical AI to forestry. The company said it will use the latest funding to support commercial deployments, deepen OEM partnerships, and continue development of supervised autonomy capabilities for complex off-road environments.

“Right now, we’re working with different forestry companies across the southeastern U.S,” Ben Pinfield, a go-to-market associate at Kodama, told The Robot Report. “We’re at a point where we’re scaling, integrating into new machine types, and developing more autonomy capabilities in forestry.”

Kodama’s technology is already deployed in commercial logging operations across the southeastern U.S. Over the past six months, machines equipped with the company’s technology have moved more than 100,000 tons of timber across multiple states.

“We’re focused on specifically plantation timber operations,” said Merritt Jenkins, co-founder and CEO of Kodama. “If we look more broadly, though, this is a tool for land management, and this is absolutely a tool that will be used in wildfire mitigation, from a forest thinning perspective, as well as wildfire suppression.”

Including the latest funding, Kodama has raised a total of $14 million to date. Konvoy Ventures and Breakwater Ventures co-led the round. The round also included participation from Blue Forest Asset Management, NYA Ventures, Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Congruent Ventures, Dangerous Ventures, M1C, and others.

The forestry industry faces tough conditions

Forest contractors are facing a lot of challenges. Demand for timber, forest management, and wildfire-resilience work is rising, but each requires long hours at remote job sites.

“If you’re a 20-something-year-old prospective logger thinking about entering the industry, you need to be on-site at 5:30 a.m., which means you’re usually leaving your home at like 4:00 or 4:30 in the morning,” Jenkins said. “Then, you’re in a machine for nine or 10 hours a day, driving over stumps and rocks and through ruts, beating up your body all day long. There are some loggers that we’ve spoken with who have gone through, for example, eight skidder operators in a year. It’s brutal turnover in this industry for this type of operator.”

As fewer people go into the industry and more operators retire, it’s getting harder and harder to find experienced, reliable operators, and fewer people want to get into the industry.

“For the heavy equipment operations, that [work] can be pretty rough on their bodies,” Pinfield said. “It’s like the bang just isn’t worth the buck as far as the physical trade-off for a lot of these operators. So, our customers are having a hard time hiring talent. Even when they are able to hire talent, a lot of times, it’s unreliable.”

What does Kodama’s technology do on job sites?

Kodama says its technology is currently running 10 to 14 hours a day on work sites. | Source: Kodama

Kodama combines supervised autonomy with teleoperation, enabling machines to handle repeatable tasks while experienced operators remotely manage complex work and edge cases. The Sonora, Calif.-based company said this hybrid approach amplifies the capabilities of skilled operators and improves machine utilization.

Kodama said it is currently working with skidders on logging sites.

“When a group of trees are cut down, a skidder with a big claw called the grapple picks them up, and drags them to the landing where they are then loaded into trucks. It’s essentially moving these trees from one place to another,” Pinfield explained. “The ultimate goal is also working on the other machines that are in those fleets, which are the cutter and the loader.”

Kodama said as it deploys more machines, its data advantage compounds through a continuous learning loop across equipment, operators, worksites, and forestry workflows.

“Every day that we remotely operate the machine, we’re generating about a terabyte of training data,” Jenkins said. “Starting two and a half years ago, we took the explicit direction of starting with teleoperation, and incrementally adding autonomy, versus autonomy first with a teleoperations failover. That’s been absolutely the right decision. Now the amount of training data that we are generating across different operating environments throughout the southeast is massive.”

Kodama works directly with existing OEMs

Merritt Jenkins, co-founder and CEO of Kodama. | Source: Kodama

Kodama is building its platform within the existing forestry-equipment ecosystem. This allows customers to adopt new operating capabilities while preserving the value of their existing machine fleets. Jenkins said the company is integrated with two of the three largest equipment manufacturers in the world.

“It’s preferable to integrate with the OEMs because you can leverage all of their knowledge and all of the sensors and fault detection that are already on the machine,” Jenkins said.

Autonomy retrofits are common in the construction world, but these are typically after-market kits. Jenkins said in the construction space, OEMs like Caterpillar create closed systems, so it isn’t possible to collaborate directly with the OEM.

What has Kodama learned from job sites so far?

Kodama has already had its technology deployed with customers in the southeast U.S. for the past two years. Pinfield said the company has been working with a customer in Georgia for over a year.

“It’s always a learning process. Every logging site is a little bit different, with different terrain and a different crew that you have to work with and introduce this new technology to them,” Pinfield said. Among the biggest benefits of automation for these site operators are reliable and consistent operations.

The team has also seen safety improvements with the technology. “Every person I spoke to on the logging sites has some kind of crazy story about how they know someone in the cab who flipped the machine, or got hurt, or a tree went flying. So, taking them out of the cab and having it be remote controlled or autonomous is a lot safer,” Pinfield said.

Looking ahead, the company plans to expand deployments and use the data it gathers to improve productivity on job sites.

“Right now, it’s several people coordinating via CB radio,” Jenkins said. “We know the real time location of our machines. We have metrics of productivity, fuel use, and the shock and vibration on the machines. So, we believe that we can eventually further optimize these sites in terms of how the machines are used and how they coordinate with each other.”

RoboBusiness 2026 kicks off tomorrow at the Santa Clara Convention Center. The event will include more than 40 sessions across five tracks: AI, Business & Development, Field Robotics, Humanoids, and Enabling Technologies. The Engineering Theater on the show floor will also feature presentations by industry experts.

Speakers at the conference will include experts from Robust AI, Agility Robotics, Amazon Robotics, Teradyne Robotics, Locus Robotics, Tesla, Boston Dynamics, ABB Robotics, MassRobotics, and more.

item.title: How to choose a BLDC motor for robotic arms and mobile robots
item.dc:creator: Faisal Mahmood
item.description:
Several factors, from sensors to safety and robotic arms or mobile platforms, help determine the selection of a brushless DC or BLDC motor.

The post How to choose a BLDC motor for robotic arms and mobile robots appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
There are several factors to choosing brushless DC or BLDC motors for robots. Source: Faisal Mahmood

Selecting a brushless DC, or BLDC, motor for robotic arms or mobile robots starts with the mechanical system, not the controller catalog. A motor rated for a particular voltage and wattage does not tell an engineer whether it can deliver the required torque at low speed, regulate position accurately, absorb regenerative energy, or survive the thermal duty cycle.

The actuator is a system. The motor, inverter, current sensors, rotor position feedback, gearbox, brake, output encoder, thermal path, communications interface, and higher level robot software all influence the result.

An industrial or collaborative robotic arm joint generally prioritizes controllable torque, low-speed smoothness, position accuracy, collision response, backdrivability, and thermal performance. A mobile robot drive motor generally puts more emphasis on efficiency, starting torque, braking, traction, battery utilization, speed regulation, and synchronization between drive channels.

The terminology also deserves care. Commercial robotics literature often uses “BLDC” and “PMSM” (permanent magnet synchronous motor) somewhat interchangeably because both are three-phase, permanent-magnet machines driven by electronic inverters. Their back EMF waveform, winding design, controller algorithm, and feedback method still determine how a particular motor behaves.

For example, STMicroelectromics treats three-phase BLDC and PMSM control as related application areas and describes both six-step and field-oriented control architectures.

Start with the mechanical load, not the controller catalog

The first selection exercise is to establish what the motor actually has to do. For a geared robotic joint, a useful first order relationship is: τ_joint = (τ_motor × gear ratio × η_gear) − τ_losses

Motor speed follows the transmission ratio: ω_motor = ω_joint × gear ratio

Mechanical power is: P_mech = τ × ω

And a first approximation of battery side electrical power is: P_elec ≈ P_mech / η_total

These equations do not replace a dynamic model, but they expose the parameters that matter before a controller is selected. Considerations include continuous torque, peak torque, peak duration, acceleration torque, gravity torque, and reflected inertia. In addition, regenerative braking, stall or near stall operation, duty cycle, thermal resistance, battery voltage range, and cable and connector current limits should all be established.

For robotic arms, the load calculation has to account for link inertia, payload, gravity compensation, gearbox ratio, backlash, compliance, counterbalance, and encoder location. A motor side encoder can report the rotor position accurately while the joint output still contains transmission error.

For mobile robots, the equivalent exercise starts with vehicle mass, wheel radius, rolling resistance, slope, acceleration, terrain, wheel slip, and drive configuration. Differential-drive platforms impose different synchronization requirements from four wheel drive vehicles. An outdoor uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) can also spend much more time in high load operation than a lightweight indoor delivery robot.

Regenerative energy deserves particular attention. During deceleration or downhill travel, the motor can return energy to the DC bus. The battery, controller, braking strategy, and bus capacitance all have to accommodate that energy. A controller that handles acceleration correctly can still create an over-voltage problem during aggressive regenerative braking.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Choose the commutation method according to motion quality

Six-step, sinusoidal, and field-oriented controls are not interchangeable labels for the same behavior.

Six-step, or trapezoidal, commutation switches the inverter through six electrical states according to rotor position. It can be attractive where implementation simplicity and cost matter or torque ripple is acceptable. It can also be suitable when the motor spends much of its operating time at moderate or high speed and precise low speed torque is not a central requirement. Hall sensors can provide the rotor position information needed for straightforward sensored implementations.

Sinusoidal control drives the phases with continuously varying current or voltage references rather than the discrete commutation states associated with basic six-step operation. It can reduce torque ripple and acoustic effects compared with a simple trapezoidal strategy, although actual performance depends on motor construction, feedback, current regulation, and tuning.

Field-oriented control, or FOC, takes the control problem further by transforming the measured phase currents into a rotating reference frame. The Clarke transformation converts the three phase quantities into a stationary two-axis representation, while the Park transformation rotates that representation into d axis and q axis components.

The controller can then regulate the components independently through current loops before transforming the command back into phase voltages and generating pulse width modulation (PWM).

In a typical PMSM application, q axis current is closely associated with torque production, while d axis current can be used for flux related control and, at higher speeds, field weakening. TI‘s motor control reference material illustrates the practical structure with Clarke and Park transformations, PI regulators, position and speed loops, and space vector PWM.

FOC is commonly attractive when the application requires smooth low-speed motion, fast torque response, or accurate speed regulation. It can also help with reduced torque ripple, regenerative braking, field weakening, or torque control for impedance and force-related behavior. FOC can therefore be a natural fit for many robotic joint and traction applications.

FOC does not automatically create a precision actuator. Rotor angle accuracy, current sense quality, motor parameter identification, sampling timing, inverter dead time, loop bandwidth, mechanical transmission, and tuning all affect the final result. A highly sophisticated algorithm cannot compensate for an encoder that is incorrectly aligned or a gearbox with substantial mechanical error.

Select the feedback architecture

Feedback selection is as important as the commutation algorithm. Hall effect sensors, incremental encoders, absolute magnetic encoders, optical encoders, resolvers, and sensorless estimation each solve different problems.

Hall sensors provide relatively coarse rotor position information and are often adequate for electronic commutation and basic speed control. They can be practical for cost-sensitive mobile platforms where the control objective does not require fine position information.

Incremental encoders provide substantially more position information and are widely used for servo control. Absolute encoders add an unambiguous position reference, which can be valuable when a robot has to know joint position immediately after startup without performing a homing sequence.

Optical encoders can provide high resolution but require appropriate mechanical and environmental protection. Magnetic encoders can offer compact packaging and tolerance for some contamination environments. Resolvers remain relevant where electrical and mechanical robustness are important.

The location of the sensor is just as important as its resolution. A motor-side encoder measures motor position. With a reduction gearbox, the output position also depends on gear ratio, backlash, compliance, torsional windup, bearing deformation, and transmission error. If those errors materially affect the task, an output side encoder can close the control loop around the actual joint position.

That does not mean every robot joint requires dual encoders. The mechanical transmission determines whether motor-side feedback provides sufficient accuracy. The Robot Report has previously covered actuator architectures using integrated servo drives and dual absolute encoders, illustrating why encoder placement becomes a system-level design issue as actuator size and performance requirements increase.

Sensorless BLDC control eliminates position sensors and their wiring, reducing cost and packaging complexity. Back EMF-based methods are established engineering techniques, and Microchip documents several implementations. The limitation is that back EMF information becomes difficult to obtain at zero and very low speed, so startup and heavily loaded low-speed operation require an appropriate strategy.

Sensorless control can therefore be useful in applications where the operating profile gives the estimator enough information, but it should not be treated as universally appropriate or inappropriate.

Match the controller to the robotic arm

A simple robotic arm joint can use a BLDC motor with Hall sensors and an external controller when the application mainly requires speed or basic position control and can tolerate relatively coarse rotor feedback. This architecture can be straightforward to commission and service, but the achievable motion quality depends heavily on the motor, gearbox, sensor resolution, controller capabilities, and higher level feedback.

A more demanding robotic joint commonly uses a BLDC or PMSM with an encoder based FOC servo drive. The drive can run a fast current loop locally, with velocity and position loops layered above it. The robot controller then commands the desired operating variable while the servo drive handles the high speed electrical control.

This architecture makes torque control practical and provides a foundation for position, velocity, impedance, and collision response strategies. Commissioning also becomes more involved. Encoder alignment, direction, current sense polarity, current loop tuning, velocity loop tuning, position loop tuning, fault thresholds, and brake timing all become part of the integration task.

An integrated robotic actuator combines some or all of the motor, gearbox, encoder, drive electronics, brake, temperature sensing, and communications interface. The attraction is obvious: fewer separate components, shorter wiring, compact packaging, and a defined interface between the actuator and robot controller.

The engineering tradeoff moves toward heat rejection, serviceability, firmware visibility, replacement strategy, and dependence on the actuator supplier.

The Robot Report‘s coverage of BLDC motors developed specifically for robot joints is one example of how motor packaging and performance requirements are increasingly considered together at the actuator level rather than as isolated motor components.

For any arm, the selection review should cover peak torque at every joint, holding torque at zero speed, brake requirements, backdrivability, and collision detection, torque estimation accuracy, and encoder placement. It should also cover gearbox efficiency, thermal soak, cable routing, mechanical compliance, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque disable or an equivalent safety function.

Match the controller to the mobile robot

BLDC motor control for mobile robots has a different emphasis because the wheels are both propulsion and contact with the environment.

A differential drive autonomous mobile robot (AMR) needs the two drive channels to track commanded velocities accurately enough for stable motion and navigation. Wheel speed feedback also contributes directly to odometry. Higher-resolution encoders become valuable when localization, synchronization, precise docking, or traction control demands more information than Hall commutation signals can provide.

Four-wheeled platforms introduce additional issues. Wheel speed matching, mechanical loading, steering or differential effects, and wheel slip can all influence control. Outdoor UGVs add water, dust, temperature changes, rough terrain, higher inertial loads, and longer periods of sustained power.

Battery behavior also changes the controller decision. Voltage sag under acceleration reduces the available electrical headroom, while regenerative braking can raise DC bus voltage. A controller designed around a nominal battery voltage therefore needs to be evaluated over the complete battery operating range rather than at one nominal value.

Thermal design is another difference. A drive enclosed inside a wheel or compact chassis may have limited airflow. The inverter, motor windings, bearings, connectors, and mechanical structure all become part of the heat path.

Harmonic Drive‘s servo-grade propulsion drive trains for AMRs illustrate this system-level relationship. Their characteristics include smooth travel, backdrivability, torque density, stiffness, and radial load support. The lesson is not that one transmission is appropriate for every AMR, but that propulsion control cannot be separated from the drivetrain.

Mobile manipulators make the distinction even more obvious. Desmasa’s MCR+ combined a robot arm and an AMR that shared one power and control architecture. The drive requirements of the base remained different from those of the arm, even though both ultimately contained electric actuators.

Evaluate current sensing and thermal behavior

Controller current ratings require careful interpretation. A datasheet may list continuous phase current, continuous bus current, peak phase current, peak current duration, RMS current, or a configurable current limit. These numbers are not interchangeable.

The motor’s thermal limit, inverter semiconductor limit, connector rating, cable rating, and battery capability can all be lower than a headline peak current specification. A controller advertised with a large peak current is therefore not automatically suitable for a motor that requires that current continuously.

BLDC.com provides a useful commercial example of the specification categories engineers encounter in controller selection. Its current controller catalog lists different input voltage ranges and current ratings across several controller families, while individual products describe interfaces and protection features.

Those specifications illustrate why engineers should compare voltage range, current definition, duration, feedback compatibility, and protection functions rather than simply comparing wattage.

The heat path must also be considered. Motor winding losses have to leave the motor through its structure and mounting arrangement. Power stage losses must leave the inverter through its enclosure, thermal interface, heat sink, airflow, or mounting structure. Thermal testing under the actual duty cycle is more informative than relying only on a short unloaded bench test.

Consider the communications and software layers

The motor controller is normally responsible for the fastest control loops. A robot controller does not need to calculate every PWM transition. Instead, the drive can execute current regulation and commutation locally while receiving higher level torque, velocity, or position commands.

Before selecting a drive, engineers should check CAN or CANopen support, EtherCAT support, RS 485 or UART, analog and PWM inputs, encoder interfaces, feedback update rates, command latency, fault reporting, firmware update procedures, parameter storage, multi axis synchronization, ROS 2 or ros2_control integration, and CiA 402 support where applicable.

CANopen’s CiA 402 profile standardizes functional behavior for servo drives and other motion control devices, including operating states and command/status structures. That can simplify interoperability when the selected hardware actually implements the required profile.

EtherCAT becomes attractive when synchronized multi axis motion and deterministic timing are central requirements. Its distributed clock architecture allows participating devices to synchronize their local timing.

ROS 2 integration is a separate consideration from the physical bus. Ros2_control represents robot hardware through command and state interfaces and provides a framework for connecting controllers to physical actuators. The controller manager also emphasizes deterministic control loop execution, showing why communication availability alone does not guarantee real time behavior.

Treat safety as an architecture, not a checkbox

A motor controller should be evaluated for overcurrent, short circuit, overvoltage, undervoltage, overtemperature, overspeed, encoder failure, Hall failure, phase loss, stall detection, brake control, communications loss, regenerative voltage rise, unintended restart, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque off where applicable.

These functions are not automatically equivalent to a complete safety architecture. Safety requirements depend on the robot category, risk assessment, operating environment, and system design.

For industrial robots, ISO 10218 1:2025 specifies safety requirements for industrial robots. ISO 13849 1:2023 addresses the design of safety related parts of control systems, including software. IEC 61800 5 2 addresses functional safety considerations for safety related adjustable speed power drive systems.

The important engineering distinction is that a controller having an overcurrent shutdown or temperature sensor does not, by itself, establish a certified safety function. The safety function has to be designed, validated, and integrated according to the applicable requirements.

A practical selection workflow

A useful motor controller selection process can be reduced to ten engineering steps.

  • Step 1: Define the complete load and motion profile, including acceleration, deceleration, payload, terrain, gravity, and duty cycle.
  • Step 2: Calculate continuous and peak torque at the motor shaft and, where applicable, at the joint or wheel.
  • Step 3: Establish the required speed, acceleration, operating range, and regenerative braking conditions.
  • Step 4: Define the control objective: speed, torque, position, impedance, or traction.
  • Step 5: Select feedback according to the actual control objective and mechanical transmission.
  • Step 6: Select six step, sinusoidal, or FOC control based on motion quality, speed range, torque requirements, and implementation constraints.
  • Step 7: Check voltage, continuous and peak current, regeneration, thermal margins, and battery behavior.
  • Step 8: Select the communication and software interfaces needed by the robot architecture.
  • Step 9: Define safety behavior, fault response, braking, communication loss behavior, and restart conditions.
  • Step 10: Validate the complete motor, drive, gearbox, sensor, brake, and robot controller as one system.

BLDC motor control selection decision table

Application requirement Preferred control direction Main reason Important limitation
Simple wheel speed control Sensored six step or simple closed loop control Low implementation complexity Coarser torque and position behavior
High-efficiency mobile traction FOC with appropriate feedback Good torque and speed regulation across a wide operating range Higher software and tuning complexity
Low-speed robotic joint motion Encoder based FOC Smooth torque production and precise rotor angle information Transmission and tuning still limit performance
High precision joint positioning Servo drive with encoder feedback, potentially output feedback Position loop can account for joint behavior More sensors, wiring, and integration effort
Torque controlled collaborative joint FOC servo architecture with suitable torque feedback or estimation Fast current/torque response Safety and torque accuracy require system validation
Sensorless high speed drive Sensorless commutation or sensorless FOC Eliminates position sensors and wiring Startup and very low speed behavior require careful design
Multi axis synchronized arm Networked servo drives, often with deterministic Ethernet Coordinated timing and distributed control Network and drive configuration become part of commissioning
Harsh outdoor mobile robot Closed loop drive with feedback selected for the environment Better speed control, diagnostics, and traction management Environmental sealing and thermal design remain system level issues

Commissioning and validation

A controller should not move directly from a wiring diagram to production operation. First, verify phase order and encoder direction. Confirm Hall or encoder alignment and current sense polarity. Run the motor unloaded at reduced voltage where the hardware permits it, then compare commanded and measured speed.

Next, check position error and current behavior. Apply a controlled mechanical load and measure phase current and bus current. Monitor motor and inverter temperatures during acceleration, steady operation, and repeated cycles.

Regenerative braking deserves a dedicated test. Measure the DC bus during controlled deceleration and confirm that the battery, braking circuit, and controller remain within their operating limits.

Communication loss testing should verify what the drive actually does when commands stop arriving. Sensor disconnection tests should confirm fault detection and the resulting state. Overcurrent, thermal protection, emergency stop, and brake behavior should also be tested under controlled conditions.

Finally, repeat the important tests after thermal soak. A drive that behaves correctly for several minutes at room temperature may behave differently after the motor and inverter reach their operating temperatures.

For a robotic arm, these tests should be performed with the gearbox and representative mechanism installed. For a mobile robot, they should include the actual wheel, vehicle mass, battery, terrain, and representative duty cycle. A bench test of an unloaded motor validates only part of the system.

Engineer’s checklist

  1. What are the continuous and peak torque requirements?
  2. What is the required speed and acceleration range?
  3. Is the objective speed, torque, position, impedance, or traction control?
  4. Is Hall feedback sufficient, or is encoder feedback required?
  5. Is motor side feedback sufficient for the mechanical transmission?
  6. Does six step control provide adequate motion quality, or is FOC justified?
  7. Are voltage, current, regeneration, and thermal margins adequate?
  8. Does the communications interface meet latency and synchronization requirements?
  9. What happens during sensor failure, communication loss, braking, and emergency stop?
  10. Has the complete actuator been tested under the actual mechanical duty cycle?

Pulling together criteria to pick the right motor

The correct BLDC motor control architecture is determined by the control variable, mechanical transmission, feedback quality, duty cycle, thermal limits, energy system, safety architecture, and software integration.

For a simple mobile drive, a sensored six-step controller may provide an adequate combination of cost, robustness, and speed regulation. A demanding robotic joint may instead require encoder based FOC, nested torque, velocity, and position loops, and possibly output side feedback.

An outdoor mobile platform may need closed loop traction control, careful regenerative energy management, environmental protection, and thermal capacity that would be unnecessary on a small indoor robot.

The key decision is therefore not simply which BLDC motor controller has the right voltage or wattage rating. The useful question is whether the complete motor, inverter, feedback system, transmission, power source, communications layer, and safety architecture can produce the required behavior throughout the robot’s actual operating envelope.

item.title: ADI explains the race to make AI physical
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
A new ADI whitepaper examines the challenges and opportunities in moving physical AI out of labs into production machinery.

The post ADI explains the race to make AI physical appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The Report Report presents a whitepaper on the race to physical AI.

AI has become remarkably good at understanding language, images, and code. The next challenge is harder — understanding reality, according to Analog Devices Inc. or ADI. Physical AI moves intelligence out of digital environments and into machines that must sense, decide, and act in the world.

Unlike software, those systems face imperfect measurements, timing constraints, changing conditions, and the consequences of action, said the company in a new report. Success will depend on more than model performance. It will require advances across sensing, simulation, computing, connectivity, and control.

In many cases, the technologies that determine whether a system succeeds sit beneath the application layer itself. A machine that shuts down when vibration crosses a preset limit is following a rule. A machine that reads vibration, temperature, current, and motor behavior; recognizes the signature of bearing wear; and adjusts before failure occurs is doing something closer to judgment.

That distinction helps explain why physical AI has become one of the most closely watched areas in technology for manufacturing. These systems do more than analyze information. They interact with the world around them, adapting to changing conditions and responding to situations that cannot be fully predicted in advance.

The next phase of physical and embodied AI is not simply about producing better answers. It is about predicting and producing useful actions in the presence of imperfect information, said ADI. To read the full whitepaper, click here: The Race to Make AI Physical.

ADI to participate in RoboBusiness 2026

Sponsored by Analog Devices Inc. Founded in 1965, the Wilmington, Mass.-based company said it combines analog, digital, AI, and software technologies to bridge the physical and digital worlds and enable breakthroughs at the intelligent edge. ADI said its semiconductors help drive advancements in automation and robotics, mobility, healthcare, energy, and data centers.

item.title: The rise of the machines is canceled: Why humanoids with AI are helpers, not enemies
item.dc:creator: Elena Krosheva
item.description:
Humans play a key role in developing humanoid robots and training AI models, so we can maintain control, writes a columnist.

The post The rise of the machines is canceled: Why humanoids with AI are helpers, not enemies appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid, shown here, is an example of a robot ready for AI.

For decades, engineers have been trying to create robots that look and act like humans. Now, rapid advances in artificial intelligence are bringing humanoid robots out of the lab and onto the factory floor. As fears grow that AI will displace workers, a global race is underway to develop humanoid robots capable of performing human work.

Competitors include Tesla, startups backed by Amazon and NVIDIA, and state-owned Chinese companies. Waltham, Mass.-based Boston Dynamics, valued at over $1 billion, is among the humanoid leaders with its Atlas robot. South Korean automaker Hyundai owns an 88% stake in the company.

Hyundai‘s massive auto plant is arguably the most advanced in the world. More than 1,000 robots work alongside nearly 1,500 humans, lifting, stamping, and welding parts in robotic unison. Atlas, at 175 cm (68.8 in.) tall and 90 kg (198.4 lb.) in weight, has left the lab and is doing real work.

Atlas and AI learn with human help

Atlas’s development is led by Zach Jackowski. He holds two degrees in mechanical engineering from MIT, and his mission is to transform the robot into a productive worker on the factory floor. Atlas confidently helps sort roof racks for the assembly line without human intervention. It operates autonomously; many roboticists would have considered this insane five or six years ago.

In 2021, Atlas was a bulky, hydraulic robot that could only run and jump. Back then, Atlas relied on algorithms written by engineers. The next-generation Atlas, with its sleek, all-electric body and AI, runs on cutting-edge NVIDIA chips, making it intelligent enough to autonomously perform incredible stunts.

Scott Kindersma led robotics research department at Boston Dynamics before moving to Google DeepMind. He explained that modern robots have learned to master movements that until recently were considered too complex for a machine. This is largely due to how these robots are programmed: more emphasis is placed on demonstrations and machine learning than on manual programming.

This humanoid can learn. Atlas learns in a variety of ways. In supervised training, machine learning specialist Kevin Bergerman (now also at Google DeepMind), wearing a virtual reality headset, took direct control of the humanoid, guiding its hand and arm movements step by step through each task until Atlas masters it. If this teleoperator can perform the task we want the robot to perform, this generates data that is subsequently used to train the robot’s AI models to perform that task autonomously.

The stylish suit you wear will actually record all your body movements to train Atlas to accurately mimic your movements. In this way, you will serve as a physical prototype for a 200-lb. metal robot. All your movements—walking, hand gestures—are captured by these sensors.

Engineers then feed this data into a machine learning process. Atlas’s body is different from yours, so they had to teach it to virtually imitate human movements. Over 4,000 digital Atlases were trained for six hours in a simulation. The simulation added complex challenges for the avatars, such as slippery floors, bending, and stiff joints.

Ultimately, this could lead to many copies of Atlas, each having loaded new skills into the AI ​​system. Once one robot is trained, they are all trained. Using the same processes, Atlas was taught to crawl and cartwheel. It wasn’t as good at duck walking.

Indeed, Atlas, or any other humanoid, can’t yet do most of the things a person does in their daily lives. For example, simply getting dressed in the morning or pouring a cup of coffee and carrying it around the house are too complex for Atlas.

What particularly stands out about Atlas is its brain. NVIDIA chips—the same ones that helped launch the AI ​​revolution with GPT chat—process a stream of collected data, bringing this humanoid robot closer to a semblance of common sense. Atlas can see its surroundings and understands how the physical world works.

One day, you’ll be able to place such a robot in a factory and simply explain to it what you want it to do. It will have enough knowledge of how the world works to perform the tasks assigned to it.

Spot platform demonstrates legged robot utility

There’s currently a lot of excitement in the industry about the potential of creating robots smart enough to be truly versatile. Robert Playter, CEO of Boston Dynamics, led the company’s robotics development until stepping down earlier this year.

The cornerstone was the robotic dog Spot, introduced almost 10 years ago. The quadruped is trained to work in hot, cold, and rugged conditions, roaming the halls of Boston Dynamics.

It has multiple cameras, thermal sensors, acoustic sensors, and an array of sensors on its back that allow it to collect data on the plant’s condition. Spot conducts quality checks at the Hyundai plant, ensuring that cars are equipped with the necessary parts. They conduct safety checks and industrial inspections at hundreds of facilities around the world. What began with Spot has evolved into Atlas. This robot is capable of superhuman movement.

Therefore, it will be able to surpass what we can do. “So, you’re creating a robot that should surpass human capabilities.”

“Why not, right? We’d love to invent creatures that could be stronger than us, withstand higher temperatures than us, or enter dangerous places.” Superhuman capabilities—for many people, that sounds terrifying. You’re not envisioning a Terminator world.

Absolutely not. If you saw how hard it takes to get robots to perform some of the simple tasks required of them, it would allay fears about intelligent and out-of-control machines. Could people have more pressing concerns?

It’s guaranteed that there will be people who say, “I’ll lose my job to a robot.” Work is truly changing. So monotonous, grueling work will eventually be performed by robots.

But these robots aren’t so autonomous that they don’t need to be managed. They need to be built, trained, and maintained. It could be several years before Atlas joins the Hyundai team permanently. Goldman Sachs predicts the humanoid robot market will reach $38 billion within a decade.

The humanoid robot race continues

Boston Dynamics and other U.S. robot makers are vying for the lead, but they’re not alone in the competition. Chinese companies are proving themselves to be formidable competitors. They’re determined to win.

Are they ahead of us?

The Chinese government is on a mission: to win the robotics race. Technically, we’re still ahead, but there’s a real risk that, simply due to the scale of our investments, we could fall behind.

To stay ahead, Hyundai has made a major investment in Boston Dynamics. This is the beginning of a long journey. The ultimate goal is the human-like future we mentioned at the beginning. Robots like us, working alongside us, walking among us.

Editor’s note: Physical AI and humanoids are among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

AI moves toward superhuman capabilities

When Demis Hassabis won the Nobel Prize in 2024, he celebrated by playing poker with the world chess champion. Hassabis loves games, which is how he became an artificial intelligence pioneer. The British scientist is co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind.

A few years ago, chatbots heralded a new era. Now, Hassabis and others are striving to create what’s known as artificial general intelligence—a silicon-based intelligence as versatile as a human, but with superhuman speed and knowledge.

“I’ve always been driven and intrigued by understanding the world around us,” said Hassabis. “Since childhood, I’ve been fascinated by big questions: the meaning of life, the nature of consciousness, the nature of reality itself.”

“I loved reading about the great scientists and philosophers who worked on these problems, and I wanted to see if we could advance human knowledge,” he recalled. “For me, the expression of this desire has been the creation of what I consider the perfect tool for advancing human knowledge: artificial intelligence.”

Hassabis noted that AI is advancing quickly, attracting attention, resources, and talent. Early chatbots only explored the internet. An app called Astra perceives the world. It was able to make up stories after being shown paintings. But such systems are still learning about context and may develop unexpected skills.

“So, new capabilities or properties may emerge as a result of learning. This may worry people,” Hassabis acknowledged. “The duality of these types of systems is that they are capable of incredible things, going beyond what we can design or understand ourselves.”

From AGI to robotics

As AI begins to take on tasks such as booking flights and shopping online, it is taking steps toward AGI. By 2030, we could have systems that truly understand their surroundings and are integrated into our daily lives. This is where robots come in.

Once a robot can perceive, understand, decide, and act, it can begin to do truly useful things. Researchers Alex Lee and Julia Vassallo have demonstrated a robot that understands what it sees. It’s not easy. And it reasons by following vague instructions. “Place the blocks whose colors correspond to the combination of yellow and blue into the corresponding ball.” The combination of yellow and blue is green. And the robot figured it out.

Is Hassabis working on a system that would be self-aware?

“I don’t think any modern system feels self-aware or, you know, conscious in any sense,” he replied. “Obviously, everyone needs to make their own decisions when interacting with these chatbots. I think it’s theoretically possible. But is self-awareness your goal? It might happen implicitly. These systems might acquire some sense of self-awareness. It’s important for these systems to understand you, themselves, and others, and that’s the beginning of self-awareness.”

“If a machine becomes self-aware, we might not recognize it,” continued Hassabis. “There are two reasons why we consider each other conscious. One is that you exhibit the behavior of a conscious being. The second is that you operate on the same foundation. We are made of the same carbon material, and our brains are soft and flexible. Machines operate on silicon. So, even if they exhibit the same behavior and say the same things, that doesn’t necessarily mean the sense of consciousness we experience is the same as theirs.”

Hassabis told us that AI could lead to what he called “radical abundance,” the elimination of scarcity. But he also gave a warning.

“There are two things that worry me. One is that malicious actors will repurpose these systems for harm,” said Hassabis. “The second question concerns the AI ​​systems themselves. As they become increasingly autonomous and powerful, can we ensure that we can control these systems, that they align with our values, that they do what we want, that they benefit society, and that they remain within established constraints?”

Can an AI agent be taught morality? “I think so,” Hassabis responded. “They learn by doing, by teaching others. And I think this is one of the challenges we must address: giving them a value system, guidance, and some constraints, just like we teach a child.”

Google DeepMind is competing with dozens of other companies striving to create AGI that you won’t be able to distinguish from human intelligence. It announced its Gemini 2 foundation model in August and Gemini 4 Argon this week.

Anduril founder says robots and AI can reduce risk

Some international groups call such weapons killer robots. But Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, said they represent the future of warfare—a working product that eliminates risks. Once a child prodigy, Luckey sold Oculus to Facebook for $2 billion.

He ultimately decided to move into the defense industry. The billionaire owns an autonomous speedboat called Dive XL. It is not remote-controlled, and Anduril claimed that it can travel 1,000 miles fully submerged. Australia has already invested $58 million in such submarines.

Tucked away inside a hangar is an Anduril unmanned fighter jet called the Fury. It has no cockpit, control stick, or rudder because there’s no pilot. Some in the defense industry viewed Anduril as just another tech startup until it beat out several leading defense contractors in the competition to build an unmanned fighter jet for the U.S. Air Force.

About the author

Elena Krosheva is a freelance journalist, marketing analyst, and SEO specialist. She graduated with honors from the Faculty of Journalism at the Institute of Modern Knowledge in Minsk, Belarus, in 2007.

Krosheva covers topics such as digitalization, IT, the modern economy, and transhumanism. She loves computers and cyberpunk, having graduated from a technical college before graduating from the Faculty of Journalism.
