The post MassRobotics opens applications for Healthcare Robotics Startup Catalyst Program appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Startups in the MassRobotics healthcare catalyst cohort will have an opportunity to showcase their technology at the Robotics Summit & Expo. | Source: MassRobotics

MassRobotics this week opened its call for applicants for Cohort 6 of its Healthcare Robotics Startup Catalyst Program. The program is a four-month, non-equity initiative that helps robotics and automation teams accelerate clinical readiness, technical validation, and go-to-market in healthcare and life sciences.

Applications are open now, and will close Dec. 31, 2026. The cohort will run February through June 2027, concluding with company showcases at the Robotics Summit & Expo in Boston.

This year, MassRobotics welcomed Intel to the program’s steering committee, joining founding partners Festo, Novanta, and Mitsubishi Electric U.S.

Intel said its Health and Life Sciences team brings mentorship and technical depth in edge AI and on-device compute for surgical and procedure-enabling robotics and OR automation, an area of growing interest across the cohort.

“Having supported the MassRobotics Healthcare Catalyst Program for three years, I’m proud of the journey we at Festo have taken — from founding member to seeing standout startups like Tenomix thrive,” said Johannes Linzbach, the head of Research Hub Boston at Festo. “What I love most is discovering the people behind the technology: their ambition, their ideas, and what drives them. At Festo, we’re excited to support Cohort 6 with our experience and connections across the ecosystem as they turn those ideas into solutions that can scale.”

Sponsors of MassRobotics’ Healthcare Robotics Startup Catalyst Program. | Source: MassRobotics

35 startups have joined the program since its start in 2021

The Healthcare Robotics Catalyst connects selected startups with senior mentors from MassRobotics’ corporate partners, along with practicing clinicians and leading organizations in the medical field. The startups work toward practical milestones such as proof-of-concept builds, pilot design, regulatory planning, or systems integration and receive organizational and technical support.

Since 2021, the catalyst program has mentored 35 startups spanning pre-seed through Series A, with teams from Boston, Toronto, and Paris to Barcelona, Sydney, and beyond. Alumni have gone on to complete a public listing, advance multiple proof-of-concept deployments, and collectively disclose more than $180 million in funding, according to MassRobotics. The organization said this reflects the program’s track record guiding healthcare robotics ventures from early prototypes to market-ready platforms.

“The MassRobotics Healthcare Catalyst Program gave us exactly what a deep-tech startup needs: direct access to people who have experienced similar problems before,” said Bingda Li, CEO of Whelix, which provides robots for cell culture automation.

“The technical support from Festo and Mitsubishi Electric US, combined with mentorship across technical development, business strategy, go-to-market, and product feedback, helped us make sharper decisions faster,” he added. “We are grateful to the MassRobotics team and the mentors who invested their time in Whelix, and we encourage other robotics startups in healthcare and life science to apply.”

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

MassRobotics describes the application process

Startups building robotics or automation for healthcare and biotech, including but not limited to laboratory and pharmaceutical automation, diagnostics and imaging workflows, hospital logistics and operating room automation, rehabilitation and assistive devices, surgical and interventional robotics, and enabling technologies such as sensing, precision motion, edge AI/on-device compute, and cybersecurity for medical devices are eligible.

The program is open to robotics startups from around the world, and both early-stage and more mature companies, including those at seed through Series C funding, are encouraged to apply. Participants will receive:

  • Tailored mentorship with senior experts from Festo, Mitsubishi Electric US, Novanta, Intel, and yaxxoo
  • Clinical perspective through the Medical Advisory Board
  • Structured onboarding, goal setting, and biweekly mentor working sessions
  • Custom workshops based on cohort needs on regulatory strategy, cybersecurity and software bills of materials (SBOMs), clinical workflow, pilot design and more
  • Visibility through MassRobotics channels and the Robotics Summit showcase in June

Applicants are evaluated on technical maturity, clinical relevance, feasibility of near-term milestones, program fit, and mentor alignment. Teams able to pursue a proof-of-concept during the four-month program are especially encouraged to apply.

After applications close, MassRobotics will hold evaluation and interviews Jan. 1 to 20, 2027. The Boston-based nonprofit will announce the Healthcare Robotics Startup Catalyst cohort on Jan. 29.

item.title: Stryker invests $400M into CMR Surgical
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff

Stryker plans to serve as the exclusive sales agent in the U.S. for the Versius robotics portfolio from CMR Surgical.

The post Stryker invests $400M into CMR Surgical appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
CMR Surgical said it designed Versius to be compact and modular, so it doesn’t require a dedicated OR. | Source: CMR Surgical

Stryker this week said it has invested about $400 million into CMR Surgical, with an exclusive option for it to acquire the company’s remaining equity. Stryker also secured an exclusive U.S. commercial agency agreement for the Versius portfolio.

“This strategic alliance is a significant milestone for CMR and a strong endorsement of the technology, clinical experience, and global business we have built,” stated Massimiliano Colella, CEO of CMR Surgical. “Stryker’s investment will give us additional strength to accelerate innovation and the continued global expansion of the Versius portfolio, while its scale and deep customer relationships create a significant growth opportunity in the United States.”

Cambridge, U.K.-based CMR Surgical said it has designed the Versius platform for real-world operating environments. The surgical robot‘s modular architecture supports flexibility across procedures, surgeon access and sites of care, the company claimed.

CMR Surgical gets clearance for more procedures

CMR Surgical said that Versius can help healthcare providers grow robotic adoption within existing operating room workflows. This scalable approach can help health systems meet growing demand for robotic-assisted surgery while preserving operational flexibility and supporting long-term program economics, added the company.

Versius supports procedures including general surgery, colorectal surgery, urology, gynecology and thoracic surgery. The robot has has been adopted in hospitals across more than 30 countries and used in 45,000 cases worldwide, according to CMR.

The Versius Plus system has earned FDA 510(k) clearance for cholecystectomy. CMR has also filed a 510(k) submission for benign gynecological indications. The robot has been used in 45,000 cases worldwide, it said.

Stryker to sell Versius system in the U.S.

“Soft-tissue robotics is a high-growth adjacency and a natural extension of Stryker’s strengths in endoscopy, visualization, and enabling technologies,” stated Andy Pierce, the group president of medsurg and neurotechnology at Stryker.

“We have evaluated the segment carefully for years, and this alliance represents a thoughtful and disciplined entry that combines the complementary strengths of both companies,” he added. “We selected CMR Surgical and the Versius portfolio because of the opportunity to help healthcare providers grow robotic-assisted surgery adoption across a broad range of procedures in hospitals and ASCs.”

“We also look forward to welcoming Andy Pierce to our board of directors and benefiting from his more than 30 years of MedTech leadership experience at Stryker as we continue expanding access to robotic-assisted surgery globally,” said Colella.

Moving forward, Stryker will serve as the exclusive U.S. sales agent for the Versius portfolio, while CMR Surgical will continue to lead portfolio development and commercialization in markets outside the United States.

Stryker’s exclusive acquisition option gives it the option of buying 100% of CMR Surgical’s outstanding equity in the future, subject to the agreement’s terms. This transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.

item.title: How ADI is helping robotics startups scale
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Jadhav
item.description:
Robotics businesses need help keeping up with innovations as they scale. Analog Devices Inc. or ADI is offering its Emerging Tech Hub.

The post How ADI is helping robotics startups scale appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The ADI cleanroom in Beaverton, Ore.

Sponsored by Analog Devices Inc.

Robotics companies are developing new capabilities at a rapid pace, from autonomous mobile robots to humanoid systems. However, keeping up with technological advances is one part of the challenge. The most critical thing is to turn a successful prototype into a commercially viable product that can be manufactured and deployed at scale. 

“The biggest challenge I see robotics startups facing today is the speed at which the industry moves,” says Cameron Villone, Senior Product Technology Manager at Analog Devices Inc. (ADI). 

In most cases, a startup excels in adopting next-generation technologies in sensing, motion control, and AI, but commercialization requires additional expertise in electronics, system integration, validation, and manufacturing. These demands can often stretch the resources of smaller engineering teams. 

ADI is developing its Emerging Tech Hub within the Analog Garage to help robotics startups and established companies overcome these challenges. The Emerging Tech Hub is intended to give companies access to ADI engineers, prototyping and testing resources, and manufacturing and sourcing expertise as they prepare their designs for production. 

The challenges of scaling robotics innovation 

ADI was recently highlighted in The Race to Make AI Physical whitepaper explaining how physical AI brings together sensing, signal conversion, perception, reasoning, control, computing, and validation. These functions must work together for a robot to perform reliably. Even when a robot makes the right decision, executing that decision depends on accurate sensor data, timely control signals, and sufficient power to drive its actuators. 

These engineering requirements continue to change as the product progresses from prototype to production. For example, a prototype needs to demonstrate whether technology can work, but commercialization requires the complete system to perform consistently under different operating conditions. 

ADI describes this through four stages: Idea, Prototype, Validate, and Scale. The initial stages focus on developing and demonstrating the concept, while validation involves testing the integrated system, identifying potential problems, and optimizing the design before production. Scaling introduces additional manufacturing and supply chain requirements. 

Robotics companies need to secure components, coordinate production, and maintain consistent quality as volumes increase. “ADI’s expansive experience in sensor development and semiconductor manufacturing allows for knowledge-driven support when these robotic developers move from idea to production,” says Villone. 

These changing demands for a robotics startup are the gaps ADI’s Emerging Tech Hub is intended to address. 

The Emerging Tech Hub brings expertise and resources 

The Emerging Tech Hub is a robotics-focused initiative being developed to bring startups and established robotics companies closer to ADI’s technical teams, including engineers implementing newly released or still-in-development technologies. 

Villone describes the approach as “co-development,” where when a company approaches the Emerging Tech Hub, the first step is to establish their current capabilities, what they are trying to achieve, and how to alginalign these goals with the Emerging Tech Hub’s mission. From there, the two sides can determine what kind of collaboration is appropriate. 

The engineering support from ADI will depend on the robotics company’s stage and needs. For example, a mature robotics developer might need a particular semiconductor component, while another may be trying to solve a different engineering problem, prompting the Emerging Tech Hub to find specialists within ADI. An early-stage startup might need broader guidance to clarify its architecture and identify what further development requires. 

The Emerging Tech Hub brings three areas of support together. The technical expertise ranges from robotics, control, edge AI, power, and system integration. Development resources include laboratories, prototyping tools, reference designs, testing and validation capabilities, and hands-on engineering support. For companies preparing to increase production, it also provides sourcing guidance and industry connections. 

Villone said ADI has recruited robotics experts from across the industry to be better equipped to handle fast paced robotic development. He cited ADI’s GMSL technology as one example of expertise that can help robotics developers address camera connectivity and integration. This support extends beyond simply component selection to decisions about how technologies fit within the wider robotic system. 

The Emerging Tech Hub is still being prepared for wider external participation, with applications expected to open by the end of 2026. 

Bridging startup agility and corporate resources 

Startups need flexibility to test ideas quickly and retain control of their technology. But working with a large technology company can introduce a tension between speed and structure. 

Villone acknowledged that some startups are reluctant to work with larger corporations because they worry about what such a relationship could mean for their business. However, he sees an opportunity when the intentions are clear. 

ADI’s interest is in enabling robotics applications using its semiconductors, while startups can benefit from expertise and resources that would be difficult to develop independently. The partnership works best when both sides understand what they want to accomplish. 

This is the same model ADI is proposing for its Emerging Tech Hub. The company describes the relationship as collaborative, with flexible, startup-friendly engagement, with the and startups retaining their intellectual property. These principles allow companies to seek technical support without surrendering ownership of their innovations. 

The same questions will be explored at RoboBusiness on October 20 during “Robotics Startup Boot Camp Part 2: Challenges & Best Practices for Working with Corporate Partners.” 

Colm Prendergast, senior director and head of the Emerging Tech Hub at ADI, will join representatives from MassRobotics and WiBotic to discuss how startups can pursue proofs of concept and pilots, how corporations evaluate potential partners, and how startup agility can coexist with corporate processes. 

The discussion aims to make those relationships more practical for companies preparing to commercialize their technologies. 

Conclusion 

A robotics company requires engineering expertise, system validation, production planning, reliable component sourcing, and industry partnerships to successfully bring the innovation to market. ADI’s Emerging Tech Hub addresses these challenges by connecting robotics companies with technical expertise and development resources. 

To learn more about building successful corporate partnerships, attend Robotics Startup Boot Camp Part 2 at RoboBusiness, where industry leaders will discuss the opportunities and challenges of working together. Register now to attend.

item.title: Agility chooses Nyobolt for ultra-fast charging for Digit 5 humanoid
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Nyobolt is providing power technology for Digit 5 that enables Agility's humanoid to work up to 20 hours a day.

The post Agility chooses Nyobolt for ultra-fast charging for Digit 5 humanoid appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Nyobolt is providing fast-charging, long-duration battery technology for Digit 5. Source: Agility

One of the challenges that humanoid robot designers face is power management. Agility Robotics Inc. today said it is working with Nyobolt on a fast-recharge battery system for its Digit 5 system. The technology will allow the robot to work more than 20 hours in a day, the companies claimed.

“For our customers, Digit’s uptime is the business case,” stated Daniel Diez, chief business officer at Agility. “Digit 5 will deliver more than 20 hours of productive work in a 24-hour day, more than two full shifts. That’s the kind of gain that materially improves the value customers get from Digit and the economics of deploying a humanoid robot fleet. Nyobolt’s ultra-fast charging technology gets us there, and it’s one of the pieces that makes Digit 5 ready for full-scale operation.”

Founded in 2015, Agility said Digit is “the first multi-purpose, human-centric robot that is ‘Made for Work’ and commercially deployed today.” The Salem, Ore.-based company said it has accumulated more than 65,000 of real-world operations. Last month, it released Digit 5 with new legs and acknowledged that it is considering wheeled locomotion.

Nyobolt builds batteries for fast charging

Founded in 2019, Nyobolt said it has combined proprietary anode materials, advanced battery cell design, and integrated power electronics to enable fast charging, high power density, reduced weight, and extended lifecycles. The Cambridge, U.K.-based company said its technology enables demanding industrial applications and reduces downtime, a key constraint in robot utilization.

Nyobolt said its patent portfolio and global footprint support AI datacenters, physical AI, and mobility applications while reducing the total cost of ownership. In May 2026, the company achieved a $1 billion valuation by raising $60 million including support from Symbotic Inc.

“Nyobolt’s technology was chosen because Digit 5 will need more power from a smaller, lighter pack in environments where reliability isn’t optional,” said Sai Shivareddy, co-founder and CEO of Nyobolt. “Agility set an exceptionally high bar for what a battery has to withstand in live warehouse and manufacturing environments, and this partnership shows what’s possible when ultra-fast charging is engineered for the toughest conditions in physical AI.”

Digit 5 features longer runtime for humanoid customers

Agility described Digit 5 as its first humanoid robot designed to work in close proximity to people safely and at scale. It will include a new battery system that delivers 90 minutes of runtime and charges in just nine minutes. This 10:1 run-to-charge ratio is an improvement from Digit 4’s 2:1 ratio.

The company asserted that this will let Digit 5 customers target longer operating windows, more productive shifts, and more demanding task sequences. Agility said this battery performance, combined with its experience with commercial deployments, will strengthen Digit’s value proposition for warehouse, distribution, and manufacturing operations.

Agility said it expects early access to Digit 5 equipped with Nyobolt’s technology to begin in the first half of 2027. Availability will increase over the following six to nine months, it added.

Agility execs prepare for merger, to speak at RoboBusiness

Agility plans to go public through a merger with special-purpose acquisition firm (SPAC) Churchill Capital Corp XI. In July, Agility opened a software and capabilities hub in Fremont, Calif., to accelerate physical AI development.
